objective: Position is an object's specific location relative to a reference point.；Velocity is a vector quantity calculated as the rate of change of position over time (Δx/Δt). Positive/negative sign indicates direction.；Acceleration is a vector quantity calculated as the rate of change of velocity over time (Δv/Δt).

questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies position as a coordinate relative to a reference point, not a change in location.

questions.stemIntent: Check if student distinguishes between position (location relative to origin) and displacement (change in position).
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think displacement equals position or that position requires displacement to be measured.
questions.stem: A car starts at a reference point and moves to a point 10 m east. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The car's final position is 10 m east of the reference point.

options.label: B
options.text: The car's displacement is 0 m because it started at the reference point.
options.feedbackWrong: Displacement is change in position, not absolute location. The car moved, so displacement is 10 m east.

options.label: C
options.text: The car's position cannot be determined without knowing the distance traveled.
options.feedbackWrong: Position is defined relative to a reference point; here the final position is known as 10 m east from the origin.

options.label: D
options.text: The car's final position is 10 m, and displacement is also 10 m so they are the same quantity.
options.feedbackWrong: Though numerically equal in this case, position is a coordinate, and displacement is a vector change. They are conceptually different.

questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that negative velocity indicates direction, not that the object is moving slowly.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
questions.alignmentNote: Velocity as a vector quantity with sign indicating direction.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student interprets negative velocity as direction only, not as 'slower'.
questions.commonMisconception: Thinking a negative velocity means the object is decelerating or moving slowly.
questions.stem: A car has a velocity of -5 m/s. What does this tell you about its motion?

options.label: A
options.text: The car is moving backwards at 5 m/s.

options.label: B
options.text: The car is moving slowly because the value is negative.
options.feedbackWrong: The magnitude is 5 m/s, so speed is 5 m/s. Negative sign indicates direction, not slowness.

options.label: C
options.text: The car is decelerating.
options.feedbackWrong: Velocity sign does not indicate acceleration. Velocity is constant here; deceleration requires a change in velocity.

options.label: D
options.text: The car's speed is -5 m/s.
options.feedbackWrong: Speed is a scalar and is always non-negative. The speed is 5 m/s, not -5 m/s.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picked wrong option on diag-sph3u-u1-0713-q1
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Confusing position with displacement; thinking position is the same as displacement or that it requires movement.

miniLesson.explain: Position is an object's specific location relative to a reference point. It is like a coordinate on a number line. Displacement is the change in position, a vector from start to finish. They are only equal if the object starts at the reference point and moves in a straight line without changing direction, but they are different concepts.
miniLesson.example: A student stands at the classroom door (reference point). They walk 5 m east to a desk. Their final position is 5 m east of the door; displacement is also 5 m east. If they then walk back to the door, final position is 0 m (at door), but displacement is -5 m east (or 5 m west) because they returned to start.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Position = 'You are here on a map.' Displacement = 'How far and in what direction you moved from start.'

guidedPractice.prompt: A soccer player kicks a ball 36 m east from the goal line. The goal line is the reference point. What is the ball's final position?
guidedPractice.answer: 36 m east of the goal line.

guidedPractice.prompt: A delivery drone starts at a warehouse (reference point). It flies 36 m north, then 18 m south. What is its final position?
guidedPractice.answer: 18 m north of the warehouse.

guidedPractice.prompt: A robot moves east at 5 m/s for 5 s, then immediately moves at -2 m/s for 3 s. What is its final position relative to its starting point?
guidedPractice.answer: 19 m east of its starting point.

reteachModules.trigger: The student selected a wrong answer on diagnostic question diag-sph3u-u1-0713-q2, indicating they think a negative velocity means slower speed.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that a negative sign on velocity indicates a slower speed, when actually the sign only indicates direction and speed is the absolute value (magnitude).

miniLesson.explain: Velocity is a vector: its sign (+ or -) tells you the direction of motion, not how fast. Speed is the magnitude (absolute value) of velocity. For example, a velocity of -2 m/s means the object is moving at 2 m/s in the negative direction – it is not 'slow' just because it's negative. A velocity of 5 m/s has a speed of 5 m/s, which is faster than 2 m/s regardless of sign.
miniLesson.example: A car moving at -2 m/s has a speed of 2 m/s. A car moving at 5 m/s has a speed of 5 m/s. The car with velocity 5 m/s is faster, even though its sign is positive. The negative sign only tells you the direction is opposite to the chosen reference.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of the sign as an arrow showing direction (e.g., left or right). The number is how fast you go. A negative number does not mean 'slow'; it means 'the other way'.

guidedPractice.prompt: A car has a velocity of -2 m/s. What is its speed?
guidedPractice.answer: 2 m/s

guidedPractice.prompt: Which car is moving faster: one with velocity 5 m/s or one with velocity -2 m/s? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: The car with velocity 5 m/s is faster. Speed is the absolute value: 5 m/s vs 2 m/s. The negative sign only indicates direction, not speed.

guidedPractice.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, a horizontal line at -2 m/s is shown. Compare its speed to a horizontal line at 5 m/s. Which line represents faster motion? Use the idea of sign and magnitude.
guidedPractice.answer: The line at 5 m/s represents faster motion because its speed (magnitude) is 5 m/s, while the line at -2 m/s has speed 2 m/s. The negative sign does not make it slower; it just indicates the opposite direction.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected incorrect definition of acceleration (change in position over time) on diagnostic question diag-sph3u-u1-0713-q3.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Misapplying acceleration as change in position over time (Δx/Δt) instead of change in velocity over time (Δv/Δt).

miniLesson.explain: Acceleration is a vector quantity that measures how quickly velocity changes. It is calculated using the formula a = Δv/Δt, where Δv is the change in velocity and Δt is the time interval. This is different from velocity, which is the rate of change of position (Δx/Δt). So, acceleration tells you how much your speed or direction changes each second.
miniLesson.example: A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to -2 m/s in 3 s. The acceleration is a = ( -2 m/s - 5 m/s ) / 3 s = -7 m/s / 3 s ≈ -2.33 m/s². The negative sign indicates acceleration opposite to the initial direction.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Acceleration = Δv/Δt, not Δx/Δt. Think 'v-change over time' — v-change is the difference in velocity, not position.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the correct formula for acceleration?
guidedPractice.answer: a = Δv/Δt

guidedPractice.prompt: A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to -2 m/s in 3 s. Calculate the acceleration.
Explain why the statement 'Acceleration is the rate of change of position over time' is incorrect.
guidedPractice.answer: That statement defines velocity, not acceleration. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time (Δv/Δt). Position change over time is velocity, which is a different concept.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answered incorrectly on diag-sph3u-u1-0713-q4, confusing slope sign with speed.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks the sign of the slope on a position-time graph indicates speed, rather than direction. They may believe a negative slope means the object is moving slowly, when speed is given by the absolute value of the slope.

miniLesson.explain: On a position-time graph, the slope represents velocity. The steepness of the slope (magnitude) tells you the speed: a steeper slope means higher speed. The sign of the slope (+ or -) tells you the direction of motion: positive slope means forward, negative slope means backward. A common mistake is to think a negative slope means slow motion; actually, a steep negative slope means fast backward motion.
miniLesson.example: Consider a graph with two segments: from t=0 to 5 s, the slope is +5 m/s (steep positive). From t=5 to 8 s, the slope is -2 m/s (gentle negative). The speed during the first segment is 5 m/s, during the second is 2 m/s. The second segment has a negative slope but lower speed. So sign indicates direction, not speed.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Slope sign tells direction; slope steepness tells speed.

guidedPractice.prompt: A position-time graph shows a line with a positive slope. What does the positive sign indicate? Choose one: a. The object is moving fast. b. The object is moving forward. c. The object is at rest.
guidedPractice.answer: b. The object is moving forward. The positive sign indicates direction, not speed. Speed is determined by how steep the line is.

guidedPractice.prompt: Consider a position-time graph with two lines: line A has a slope of +3 m/s, line B has a slope of -5 m/s. Which line represents a higher speed? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: Line B has a higher speed because the magnitude (absolute value) of its slope is 5 m/s, which is greater than 3 m/s. The negative sign only indicates that line B is moving backward. So line B is faster, despite being negative.

guidedPractice.prompt: An object moves in two segments: first 5 s at +5 m/s, then 3 s at -2 m/s. What is the total displacement? Which segment had greater speed? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: Displacement = (5 m/s × 5 s) + (-2 m/s × 3 s) = 25 m - 6 m = 19 m. The first segment had greater speed (5 m/s > 2 m/s). Speed is the absolute slope value, not the sign. The first segment's positive slope is steeper, so higher speed.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects option that says area under v-t graph equals distance rather than displacement.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student mistakenly thinks the area under a velocity-time graph always gives the total distance traveled, ignoring that areas below the axis (negative velocity) represent motion in the opposite direction and should be subtracted to find displacement.

miniLesson.explain: The area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement, which is the net change in position, not the total distance traveled. Displacement accounts for direction: areas above the time axis are positive (forward motion), areas below are negative (backward motion). Distance would be the sum of the absolute values of these areas.
miniLesson.example: Consider an object moving at 5 m/s for 30 s (forward) then at -2 m/s for 30 s (backward). The displacement is (5 m/s × 30 s) + (-2 m/s × 30 s) = 150 m - 60 m = 90 m. The total distance traveled is |5|×30 + |-2|×30 = 150 + 60 = 210 m. Notice displacement (90 m) is not the same as distance (210 m).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Area under v-t = Δx (displacement), not total distance. Remember: + and - cancel; for distance, use absolute values.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
guidedPractice.answer: Displacement

guidedPractice.prompt: An object moves at 4 m/s for 10 s, then at -3 m/s for 5 s. Calculate the displacement.
An object moves at 6 m/s for 2 s, then at -4 m/s for 3 s, then at 0 m/s for 1 s. What is the displacement and total distance?

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Assuming acceleration-time graphs in Grade 11 can show non-constant acceleration.

miniLesson.explain: In Grade 11 Physics, acceleration-time graphs only cover scenarios where acceleration is constant. The graph is a horizontal line. The area under the graph equals the total change in velocity.
miniLesson.example: Consider the segment where an object moves at constant velocity -2 m/s for 3 s. Its acceleration is constant at 0 m/s². The a-t graph is a horizontal line at a=0. The area under that line (height 0 times width 3 s) is 0 m/s, which equals the change in velocity (since velocity is constant).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Grade 11 a-t graphs are always flat lines – constant acceleration only.

guidedPractice.prompt: What shape does an acceleration-time graph have in Grade 11 Physics?
guidedPractice.answer: A horizontal line (constant acceleration).

guidedPractice.prompt: If an object has a constant acceleration of 0 m/s² for 3 s, what is the change in velocity?
guidedPractice.answer: 0 m/s.

guidedPractice.prompt: Describe the motion of an object whose acceleration-time graph is a horizontal line at a = 0 for a time interval of 3 s.
guidedPractice.answer: The object moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration) during that interval.

reteachModules.trigger: The five equations of motion only apply when acceleration is uniform (constant).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The five core equations for uniform acceleration (v = v₀ + at, Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt², etc.) are applied to situations where acceleration is not constant, leading to incorrect results. Students may think these equations always work regardless of the motion's nature.

miniLesson.explain: The five kinematic equations are derived assuming constant acceleration (uniform). If acceleration changes over time, these equations no longer accurately describe the motion. For example, in a velocity-time graph, the equations assume a straight line (constant slope). If acceleration varies, the graph curves, and the simple formulas fail.
miniLesson.example: Consider an object moving at 5 m/s for 3 s, then instantly switching to -2 m/s for 3 s. The acceleration is not constant (infinite at the switch). Using Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt² for the entire 6 s would be invalid. Only the total displacement of 19 m can be computed piecewise (5 m/s for 3 s gives 15 m, then -2 m/s for 3 s gives -6 m, total 9 m? Wait, 15 + (-6) = 9 m, but lesson says total displacement 19 m? Actually from lesson: 5 s at 5 m/s then 3 s at -2 m/s gives 25 - 6 = 19 m. But using 3 s each: 15 - 6 = 9 m. So the example is different. I'll use the lesson's two-phase: 5 s at 5 m/s gives 25 m, 3 s at -2 m/s gives -6 m, sum 19 m. The acceleration is zero in each phase but changes at the boundary, so not uniform overall.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: U.A. only! The five equations are only for Uniform Acceleration.

guidedPractice.prompt: Under what condition can you use the five kinematic equations (e.g., v = v₀ + at, Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt²)?
guidedPractice.answer: Acceleration must be constant (uniform).

guidedPractice.prompt: A car travels at 5 m/s for 3 s, then instantly changes to -2 m/s for another 3 s. Can you use the equation Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt² for the entire 6 s motion? Explain why or why not.
guidedPractice.answer: No, because the acceleration is not constant. During the first 3 s, acceleration is 0 m/s²; during the last 3 s, acceleration is also 0 m/s², but at the instant of change, acceleration is undefined (infinite). The overall acceleration is not uniform, so the equation does not apply to the full interval.

guidedPractice.prompt: Given that an object experiences constant acceleration and its displacement over 30 s is 90 m, and its initial velocity is 6 m/s, calculate the acceleration using an appropriate equation. (Use numbers from the lesson: 90 m, 30 s, 6 m/s.)
guidedPractice.answer: Using Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt²: 90 = 6*30 + ½a*(30)² = 180 + ½a*900 = 180 + 450a. So 90 - 180 = -90 = 450a, thus a = -90/450 = -0.2 m/s². (Note: The numbers are from the lesson's segmented motion, but this example assumes constant acceleration from the start. The answer is consistent with the data.)

questions.stem: A cat is initially 6 m east of a fire hydrant (reference point). It then runs another 18 m east. What is the cat's final position?
In the same scenario, what is the cat's displacement? In one sentence, explain how displacement differs from position.
questions.rubric: Displacement is 18 m east. Position is the location relative to a reference point (final position 24 m east), while displacement is the change in position (18 m east). They are different because position depends on the initial location relative to the reference, whereas displacement only depends on the movement.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly: single choice correct and open-ended answer must state displacement = 18 m east and at least mention that position is location relative to a reference while displacement is change in position.

questions.stem: A car has a velocity of -2 m/s. What is its speed?

In a two-phase motion, an object moves at 5 m/s for 5 seconds, then at -2 m/s for 3 seconds. Compare the speeds during the two phases. Is the negative velocity slower? Explain using the concepts of velocity and speed.
questions.rubric: The student must state: Speed is the magnitude (absolute value) of velocity. During the first phase, speed = 5 m/s; during the second phase, speed = 2 m/s. Therefore, the first phase is faster. The negative sign in -2 m/s only indicates direction, not speed.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly to pass.

questions.stem: Which formula correctly represents acceleration?
A cyclist's velocity changes from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 seconds. Calculate the acceleration. Then, in one sentence, explain why acceleration uses change in velocity rather than change in position.
questions.rubric: Calculation: a = (8 - 2) / 3 = 6 / 3 = 2 m/s². Explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not position; position change over time is velocity.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 correct AND Q2 calculation correct (2 m/s²) AND explanation correctly distinguishes Δv/Δt from Δx/Δt.

questions.stem: On a position-time graph, line A has a slope of +3 m/s and line B has a slope of -5 m/s. Which line represents a higher speed?
options: Line A, because positive slope means faster.
Line B, because the magnitude of its slope is larger.
Both have the same speed because speed is always positive.
Line A, because it is moving forward.

questions.stem: Explain why a negative slope on a position-time graph does not necessarily indicate slow motion. Use the concept of slope magnitude and sign in your answer.
questions.rubric: Student must state that speed is determined by the absolute value (magnitude) of the slope, and the sign indicates direction only. A negative slope can be steep (e.g., -10 m/s) which means fast backward motion.

questions.stem: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
An object moves at 5 m/s for 3 seconds, then at -2 m/s for 30 seconds. What is the displacement? Show your calculation.
questions.rubric: Correct displacement of -45 m (or 45 m in the opposite direction) with signed area calculation: (5 m/s × 3 s) + (-2 m/s × 30 s) = 15 m - 60 m = -45 m. Accept absolute value if direction is explained.

retestCards.passRule: Answer question 1 correctly (option 0) and provide a correct displacement calculation in question 2.

questions.stem: In Grade 11 Physics, which statement about acceleration-time graphs is correct?
options: They can show any type of acceleration.

questions.stem: Explain why acceleration-time graphs in Grade 11 are restricted to constant acceleration. In your explanation, describe what the area under such a graph represents.
questions.rubric: Must state that Grade 11 only covers constant acceleration, so the graph is a horizontal line; area under the graph equals change in velocity.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 correct AND Q2 includes both 'constant acceleration' and 'area equals change in velocity'.

questions.stem: In which situation can the equation v² = v₀² + 2aΔd be correctly used to find final velocity?
options: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 5 m/s over 3 s.
A ball thrown upward with constant gravitational acceleration.
A car moves at 5 m/s for 5 s, then instantly changes to -2 m/s for 3 s.
A train moves at constant velocity 5 m/s for 3 s, then accelerates uniformly for 3 s.

questions.stem: Calculate the total displacement of an object that moves at 5 m/s for 5 s, then immediately at -2 m/s for 3 s. Explain why the equation Δd = v₀t + ½aΔt² cannot be applied to the entire 8-second interval.
questions.rubric: Displacement = 5*5 + (-2)*3 = 25 - 6 = 19 m. Explanation: Acceleration is not constant over the 8 s; it changes abruptly at t=5 s from 0 m/s² to 0 m/s² but with an infinite spike, so the uniform acceleration equation does not apply for the full interval.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions answered correctly; for open-ended, answer must include correct displacement (19 m) and mention non-constant acceleration or instant change.

teacherEscalation.condition: student fails the same retest twice or scores in the lowest tier on two consecutive lesson diagnostics
teacherEscalation.message: 该学生需要人工短辅导；问题不是单题错误，而是核心概念系统没有建立。

dashboardFormat.objective: Position is an object's specific location relative to a reference point.；Velocity is a vector quantity calculated as the rate of change of position over time (Δx/Δt). Positive/negative sign indicates direction.；Acceleration is a vector quantity calculated as the rate of change of velocity over time (Δv/Δt).

learningGoals.statement: Distinguish between position and displacement, and correctly define velocity and acceleration as vector quantities.
Interpret position-time graphs: slope steepness indicates speed, sign indicates direction.
Interpret velocity-time graphs: area under the curve equals displacement, absolute value equals speed.
Recognize that acceleration-time graphs in Grade 11 only cover constant acceleration.
Select and apply the five uniform acceleration equations to solve motion problems.

cards.question: A car starts at a reference point and moves to a point 10 m east. Which statement is correct?
options: The car's final position is 10 m east of the reference point.
The car's displacement is 0 m because it started at the reference point.
The car's position cannot be determined without knowing the distance traveled.
The car's final position is 10 m, and displacement is also 10 m so they are the same quantity.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student distinguishes between position (location relative to origin) and displacement (change in position).
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Displacement is change in position, not absolute location. The car moved, so displacement is 10 m east.
Position is defined relative to a reference point; here the final position is known as 10 m east from the origin.
Though numerically equal in this case, position is a coordinate, and displacement is a vector change. They are conceptually different.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies position as a coordinate relative to a reference point, not a change in location.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Position is a fundamental concept of understanding motion in one dimension.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think displacement equals position or that position requires displacement to be measured.

cards.question: A car has a velocity of -5 m/s. What does this tell you about its motion?
options: The car is moving backwards at 5 m/s.
The car is moving slowly because the value is negative.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student interprets negative velocity as direction only, not as 'slower'.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The magnitude is 5 m/s, so speed is 5 m/s. Negative sign indicates direction, not slowness.
Velocity sign does not indicate acceleration. Velocity is constant here; deceleration requires a change in velocity.
Speed is a scalar and is always non-negative. The speed is 5 m/s, not -5 m/s.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that negative velocity indicates direction, not that the object is moving slowly.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Velocity as a vector quantity with sign indicating direction.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking a negative velocity means the object is decelerating or moving slowly.

cards.question: Acceleration is calculated as:
options: Change in velocity divided by time interval
Change in position divided by time interval
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the correct formula for acceleration (∆v/∆t) not (∆x/∆t).
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
That is average velocity, not acceleration.
Acceleration depends on change in velocity, not just final velocity.
Speed is scalar; acceleration is vector and uses velocity.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly defines acceleration as change in velocity over time, not change in position over time.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Acceleration is a key concept in understanding motion.
cards.commonMisconception: Confusing acceleration with velocity; thinking acceleration is rate of change of position.

cards.question: In a position-time graph, a line with a negative slope indicates:
options: The object is moving backwards (opposite direction).
The object is moving slower than if the slope were positive.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student correctly interprets slope on a position-time graph as velocity, not speed.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Speed is related to absolute slope value, not sign. A steep negative slope means fast backwards motion.
Slope indicates velocity, not acceleration. Deceleration would appear as curvature.
A horizontal line indicates rest; a negative slope means motion.
cards.successCriteria: Interprets slope sign as direction and steepness as speed on a position-time graph.
cards.ossdExpectation: Investigate uniform and non-uniform linear motion in qualitative and quantitative terms, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Position-time graph analysis is part of investigating motion.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking a negative slope means slower speed rather than opposite direction.

cards.question: The area under a velocity-time graph represents:
options: Total distance traveled by the object.
Change in velocity of the object.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows that area under v-t graph gives displacement (a vector), not necessarily total distance.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Displacement considers direction; area above axis is positive, below negative. Distance would be sum of absolute areas.
Acceleration is slope of v-t graph, not area.
Change in velocity is area under acceleration-time graph, not velocity-time graph.
cards.successCriteria: Identifies that area under velocity-time graph gives displacement, not distance.
cards.ossdExpectation: Investigate uniform and non-uniform linear motion in qualitative and quantitative terms, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Velocity-time graph interpretation is essential for problem solving.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking area under v-t graph always gives distance traveled, neglecting sign cancellation.

cards.question: In Grade 11 Physics, acceleration-time graphs typically show:
options: Any type of acceleration, including changing acceleration.
Acceleration as a function of time with linear changes.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the grade-level scope: only constant acceleration a-t graphs.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Non-constant acceleration is not covered in the Grade 11 curriculum.
Acceleration can be negative (deceleration) even with constant acceleration.
That would be non-constant acceleration, which is beyond the scope.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that a-t graphs in Grade 11 are limited to constant acceleration scenarios.
cards.ossdExpectation: Investigate uniform and non-uniform linear motion in qualitative and quantitative terms, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Acceleration-time graph analysis is part of investigating motion, but scope is restricted.
cards.commonMisconception: Assuming that any shape of a-t graph is covered in Grade 11.

cards.question: Explain under what condition the five core equations for uniform acceleration (e.g., v = v₀ + at, Δd = v₀t + ½at²) are valid. Why is that condition necessary?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student recognizes the limitation of the five equations: they are only valid for constant acceleration.
cards.successCriteria: States that the five equations of motion only apply when acceleration is constant (uniform).
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Understanding the condition for using uniform acceleration equations.
cards.commonMisconception: Applying the equations to non-uniform acceleration without recognizing they are not valid.
